beats.narration_text: Hi, I'm Sai Pranavi J. This video is about context window limits, the fixed, hard-capped budget every prompt has to fit inside, measured in tokens, not words or characters, and three questions for telling what actually happens when you go over it.
beats.new_visual_element: Personal-intro card: fellow's name + one-line summary of what the video covers, spoken

shot.note: Same pattern as this fellow's other episodes' B01; opens with the required FELLOWS-SUBMISSION.md intro line.

beats.narration_text: Every prompt you send shares one fixed pool, the instructions, any document you paste in, the whole conversation so far, even the room left over for the model's own answer. That pool doesn't grow. It's measured in tokens, rough chunks of text, not characters, not words, so counting by eye is already a guess. Fill it past the edge, and something has to give.
beats.new_visual_element: A generic context-window budget panel filling up row by row, then an overlay posing the real question: full, did it tell you?

shot.note: Generic/hypothetical context-window panel, no real model, vendor, or system named, per FACTCHECK.md.

beats.narration_text: Here's the test, before any example: three questions. One, count the tokens: is this budget actually measured in tokens, the model's own unit, not the characters or words you'd eyeball it with? Two, share the pool: everything competing for room, the system instructions, any retrieved documents, the conversation history, and the model's own output, draws from that one fixed budget, not separate ones. Three, watch the edge: when the total goes over, does the system refuse outright, or does it quietly drop something and keep going? A budget you can't see filling up is a budget you can't manage.
beats.new_visual_element: Checklist card, all 3 tests shown together (Count the Tokens / Share the Pool / Watch the Edge)

shot.note: Framework shown fully before any example, matching prior STEM videos' rubric beat.

beats.narration_text: Here's how it actually works. Picture a context window sized, for this illustration, at one thousand tokens. System instructions take a fixed hundred and fifty. A long document you've pasted in takes seven hundred more. That already leaves only a sliver of room for the conversation so far, and for the model's own reply. Keep the conversation going, and that history keeps growing, past the room that's actually left. One common way systems handle this, they quietly drop the oldest turns to make room, say nothing about it, and answer anyway.
beats.new_visual_element: A fixed budget, its competing consumers (instructions, document, growing history), and what gets silently dropped, all shown together, tagged TRUNCATED SILENTLY

shot.note: [Source: FACTCHECK.md #3/#4 -- generic illustration of a well-documented architectural pattern, no real model/vendor named] The budget, the competing consumers, and the thing that quietly disappears must all be visible together so the mechanism reads without narration alone.

beats.narration_text: Now the case that would break this test if it were sloppy: the exact same budget, the same document, the same growing conversation. But this system checks the total before it answers, and when that total would go over, it refuses outright, one clear error, no answer, nothing quietly dropped. The limit got hit just as hard as before. The difference was never whether you went over, it's whether the system told you.
beats.new_visual_element: The same fixed budget and the same overflow as B04, but the system checks the total before answering and refuses outright with an explicit error instead of dropping anything, tagged CAUGHT IMMEDIATELY

shot.note: [Source: FACTCHECK.md #3 -- generic illustration, no real model/vendor named] Stress-tests the framework: the only variable changed from B04 is whether the system checks the total before answering.

beats.narration_text: Here's something to try today. Pick any system you already use that has a length or size limit, a chat app, an upload form, an API call. Deliberately go a little over it, on purpose. Watch what happens, does it refuse clearly, or does it just keep going? If something got silently dropped, figure out exactly what, the oldest message, the middle of your document, the end of your prompt. This isn't unique to language models either, it happens anywhere a sender doesn't know what the receiver can actually hold.
beats.new_visual_element: The 3-question rubric restated as a concrete, actionable checklist, distinct from B03's framework card

shot.note: Generic real-world tie-in sentence only (no specific project/company/bug named), per FACTCHECK.md.

beats.narration_text: A context window isn't elastic. It's a fixed budget, shared by everything you put in and everything you ask for back. Going over it was never really the question. Whether the system tells you when you do, that's the one that matters.
